extracted.intended_audience: Congress and patent stakeholders (policymakers, practitioners, industry, academics)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of the current U.S. patent-eligibility (§101/Alice–Mayo) jurisprudence and related USPTO guidance, focusing on clarity, predictability, effects on innovation, investment, competition, patent quality, and legal costs. Intended to inform policy decisions and potential reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current law is sufficiently clear, predictable, and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that current case law provides clarity, predictability, and consistency in patent-eligibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support cited: Federal Circuit affirms ineligibility decisions at a high rate; USPTO report 'Adjusting to Alice' shows similar rejection rates pre- and post-Alice; an AI system was trained to predict Alice outcomes with reasonable accuracy. Commenters (e.g., CCIA, Dell, IBM, Johnson & Johnson) argued that modern case law and recent decisions have clarified essential boundaries and produced a predictable standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current law is unclear and unpredictable
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that current jurisprudence is fundamentally unsettled, unpredictable, and indeterminate, making eligibility outcomes difficult to foresee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms include reliance on subjective reasoning to determine 'abstract' concepts, varying outcomes across courts and art units, and judicial commentary describing the doctrine as incoherent or destabilizing. Examples and citations: remarks by Federal Circuit judges (e.g., Chief Judge Kimberly Moore, Judges Plager, Linn, Newman), and concern over variance in district court grant rates for motions to dismiss on eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity/arbitrariness of the 'abstract' determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (or other judicial exception) are subjective and can be arbitrary without clearer guideposts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes that courts have not adequately defined 'abstract,' so determining if a claim is 'something more' than the undefined abstract is difficult and often arbitrary. Commenters observed that this subjective judgment relies heavily on fact-specific prior decisions, producing inconsistent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertain trajectory threatening traditionally patentable technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent eligibility cases may be expanding judicial exceptions into technologies historically considered patentable (e.g., mechanical technologies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters referenced cases such as American Axle v. Neapco and Yu v. Apple and noted holdings finding ineligible subject matter in mechanical device contexts (e.g., electric car charger, garage door opener, driveshaft tuning, camera design), raising concern no technical field is safe from eligibility challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of USPTO guidance: not binding on courts
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance and examiner instructions have limited effect because they are not binding on federal courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters said that even when applicants follow USPTO guidance to obtain patents, courts may take materially different views of eligibility, leaving patents vulnerable to invalidation. Citations include AIPLA, AUTM, IPO, and Innovation Alliance observations that USPTO guidance cannot resolve problems caused by Alice–Mayo in courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of USPTO guidance: inconsistent examiner application
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO examiners have not applied the guidance uniformly, leading to variability in prosecution outcomes depending on examiner or art unit assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners reported that different examiners—even within the same art unit—hold vastly different interpretations. Commenters noted assignment to a particular technology art unit can be a significant determinant of review outcomes and prosecution difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that USPTO guidance exceeds Supreme Court precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's revised guidance may diverge from or exceed the reach of Supreme Court precedent, potentially leading to improperly issued patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters argued the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance changed course from earlier USPTO guidance and may be inconsistent with Alice, resulting in thousands of improperly issued patents that then require expensive post-grant reviews to correct. Concerns about undermining the presumption of validity were raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current jurisprudence improves patent quality and public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that eligibility jurisprudence forces applicants to better define inventions, improving patent quality and useful public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters (e.g., CCIA, Google) stated the eligibility test acts as a 'forcing function' leading to greater detail and clarity in patent applications, thereby providing more useful information to the public and clearer claim boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on innovation — jurisprudence is beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that exclusions from patentability (laws/products/abstract ideas) play a crucial role in fostering technological invention and public-benefiting research by keeping basic tools free for follow-on work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil liberties and public-interest commenters argued expanding eligibility to basic tools would impede innovation; examples include free access to genomic information during COVID-19. Some claimed the current regime prevents overbroad patents by NPEs, preserving resources for productive innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on innovation — jurisprudence is detrimental (especially life sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that current eligibility jurisprudence undermines innovation in certain technologies (notably life sciences), jeopardizing development of diagnostics, precision medicine, and pharmaceuticals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry commenters (BIO, PhRMA, Novartis, Johnson & Johnson) argued uncertainty discourages costly, long-term investment required for drug and diagnostic development, potentially decreasing innovation and leading to fewer new products reaching market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on investment — little/no negative effect in some tech sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Some industry commenters assert that investment (e.g., in AI and startups) continues to boom despite current jurisprudence, indicating little adverse effect on capital flows in certain sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: record funding for AI firms cited (Q2 2021), continued upward trends in investment post-Alice in some emerging technologies. Commenters used these data to argue that §101 uncertainty has not chilled investment broadly, at least in certain computer-related fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on investment — negative effects in life sciences and high-cost R&D fields
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that eligibility uncertainty reduces investment in high-cost, high-risk fields (biologics, diagnostics), because investors require reliable patent protection to justify large expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted drug development costs ($2B and 8–12 years) and diagnostic development costs (~$100M and 7–10 years) as examples where uncertainty in patent protection could deter investment and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on competition — promotes competition by curbing overbroad patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that current jurisprudence is pro-competitive by preventing overbroad patents and protecting startups and SMEs from abusive litigation by NPEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software/internet organizations argued that limiting abstract-idea patents reduces litigation costs and democratizes participation in AI and other areas by protecting less-resourced entities from overbroad assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on competition — undermines competition and advantages incumbents
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that eligibility uncertainty harms startups and SMEs' ability to attract investment and defend market positions, leading to consolidation and concentration among large incumbents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters (e.g., Innovation Alliance, USIJ, Ericsson) argued diminished enforceable patents reduce startups' leverage, hindering licensing, reducing new entrants, and potentially limiting competition in sectors such as diagnostics and digital technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on legal costs — mixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Current jurisprudence can both reduce abusive litigation (lowering some legal costs) and increase costs associated with prosecution, post-issuance litigation, and strategy development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters noted reductions in NPE-driven litigation; many others reported higher prosecution difficulty and expense, higher post-issuance litigation costs, and greater expenditures to develop legal strategies in light of eligibility uncertainty.
